why.text: In Lucknow on Diwali night 2020, fine particles (PM2.5) reached 352 µg/m³, about 3.5 times the level on the night before, and carried metals such as lead, cadmium and arsenic.
A study of Delhi's air from 2013 to 2017 found that Diwali firecrackers cause a small but statistically significant rise in PM2.5, on top of winter smog from other sources.
Videos of pet dogs on New Year's Eve showed clear fear during fireworks: ears pulled back, pacing and panting.
In a survey of 13,700 dogs, sensitivity to noise such as fireworks was the most common anxiety, affecting 32%.

instead: Light lamps and candles, and decorate with flowers and rangoli.
Go to one shared, short community display instead of many private ones, or skip fireworks entirely.
Celebrate a win with music at a safe volume, food and a gathering.
Keep pets indoors and calm, and check on older neighbours and people with asthma.

practice: Very loud music, DJs and loudspeakers

why.text: The WHO lists exposure to loud sounds among the preventable causes of hearing loss, and says over 1 billion young adults risk permanent, avoidable hearing loss from unsafe listening.
Sensitivity to noise is the most common anxiety in pet dogs, affecting about a third of them.

instead: Keep the volume at a level where people can still talk.
Point speakers away from homes, hospitals and schools, and stop at night.
Choose live, acoustic music for processions.

why.text: In a study of 1,733 dead seabirds, balloons were the deadliest debris they swallowed: 32 times more likely to kill than hard plastic.

instead: Decorate with paper, cloth, flowers or lights you can reuse.
Never release balloons into the sky.
Blow bubbles or plant a tree to mark the day.

practice: Single-use plastic plates, decorations and packaging

why.text: India generated over 34 lakh tonnes of plastic waste in 2019-20.
World plastic production has more than doubled in two decades, and plastic pollution depends mostly on how waste is handled.

instead: Use steel plates, leaf plates or washable crockery, and ask guests to bring a bottle.
Reuse decorations every year.
Give gifts without plastic wrapping, or give an experience instead of a thing.

practice: Cooking far more food than people can eat

why.text: Christmas, Easter, other religious celebrations and holidays make households buy and cook more food than they need, which adds to avoidable food waste.

instead: Plan the menu for the number of guests who confirm.
Serve smaller portions and let people come back for more.
Share leftovers with neighbours, workers and food banks the same day.

why.text: Alcohol caused about 2.6 million deaths worldwide in 2019, including 700,000 from injuries such as road crashes and violence.

instead: Host alcohol-free celebrations, or keep good soft drinks for everyone.
Never pressure a guest to drink.
Never drive after drinking; plan a sober driver or a cab.

practice: Immersing plaster or painted idols in lakes, rivers and the sea
occasions: Other festivals that end with immersion

why.text: After idol immersion in three Nagpur lakes, lead, cadmium, copper, iron and manganese in the water and in tilapia fish rose above safe limits, making the fish unsafe to eat.

instead: Choose an unpainted idol of natural clay, or one coloured with natural dyes.
Immerse it in a bucket or a city's artificial tank, and use the clay in a garden.
Keep a metal or stone idol and worship it every year.

why.text: Holi powders bought in Kolkata had about twice the lead allowed in cosmetics, and endotoxin levels about 35 times the safe reference. Such powders are often sold as herbal, with no checks on what they contain.

instead: Use colours made from flowers, turmeric, beetroot or spinach.
Play a dry Holi to save water.
Only put colour on people who say yes, and never on animals.

why.text: Doctors in northern India recorded 26 kite-string injuries in two years, some of them fatal cuts to the neck and face. They note that birds, especially raptors and pigeons, are often caught and maimed or killed.
The same study notes that a 2017 National Green Tribunal order told every state to ban synthetic and glass-coated manjha.

instead: Fly kites only with plain cotton thread.
Avoid flying early in the morning and at dusk, when birds are most active.
Collect broken string from trees and roofs, and call a bird rescue group for injured birds.

practice: Killing animals as a religious offering
occasions: Some Durga Puja and Kali Puja observances
Some temple and village deity festivals

why.text: The world animal health body lists the welfare risks animals face around slaughter: rough handling, unfamiliar noise and surroundings, forced movement, crowding, and stunning or bleeding that is not done properly.
A review of rituals and infection links ritual animal sacrifice to diseases that pass from animals to people, including brucellosis, cutaneous anthrax, orf and bovine tuberculosis.

instead: Give the value of the animal to people in need, in money or food.
Share a plant-based feast with family, neighbours and the poor.
Make a symbolic offering, such as a coconut, fruit or sweets.

practice: Bull taming, races and other animal contests

why.text: At one Madurai hospital, 42 people came in with bull injuries in under two years; 59% were hurt while taking part in sporting events such as Jallikattu, most of them with penetrating wounds.

instead: Honour cattle by caring for them: feeding, rest and vet care.
Hold contests between people, such as races and games, not with animals.

practice: Eating meat, dairy and eggs every day

why.text: Livestock supply chains produce 14.5% of all human-caused greenhouse gases.
Nearly all beef and lamb has a higher carbon footprint than plant-based alternatives, even from the lowest-impact farms.
The welfare risks animals face at slaughter are the same whether the meat is for a festival or an ordinary day.

instead: Make more meals plant-based: dal, beans, vegetables, grains and nuts.
Try plant milks and dairy-free sweets.
Choose a vegetarian or vegan menu for weddings and parties.

practice: Whipping or cutting your own body in rituals

why.text: Self-flagellation with sharp instruments draws blood. It is practised by some Shia Muslims at Muharram and by some Christian groups, and has been linked to HTLV-1 and hepatitis C infections.
Ten men in the UK caught HTLV-1, a virus that can lead to leukaemia, with self-flagellation the only risk factor found; the virus then passed to partners.

instead: Mourn and remember through prayer, recitation and processions without blades.
Organise a blood donation camp, so the blood given saves lives.
Never share blades or chains.

why.text: At least 1.5 million girls under 18 are married in India each year. A child bride is more likely to face domestic violence and to die from complications of pregnancy and childbirth.
23% of women aged 20 to 24 were married before 18 in 2019-21.

instead: Keep girls in school, and wait until both people are adults and choose to marry.
Report a child marriage to Childline on 1098.

why.text: Dowry was banned in 1961 but is still widely paid: a survey of 5,206 married adolescent girls in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar found it still prevalent.
In a national study of 23,785 women, districts where dowry became more common saw women's health get worse.

instead: Refuse to give or take dowry, and say so openly.
Have a simple wedding, with costs shared equally by both families.

practice: Ending a marriage by saying talaq three times

why.text: With instant triple talaq a husband can end the marriage on his own, with no legal process and no say for the wife, and women, especially poorer women, suffer most.
why.source: Asian Journal of Research in Social Sciences and Humanities (2017)

instead: Give husband and wife the same rights and process to end a marriage.
Try counselling and family mediation first.
Make sure maintenance and custody are settled fairly.

why.text: More than 230 million girls and women alive today have undergone genital cutting. It has no health benefits and can cause severe bleeding, infections and problems in childbirth, and it violates girls' human rights.

In South Asia it is known as khatna or sunna. A study in Sri Lanka, which included Dawoodi Bohra and other Muslim communities, found it is mostly done by older women using blades, and sometimes secretly by doctors.

instead: Leave girls' bodies uncut.
Mark a child's birth or coming of age with a prayer, a meal or a gift.
Talk to a doctor, and support community members who speak against it.

occasions: Temple and other places of worship
Everyday household rules in many communities

why.text: A study of women of different religions in Jammu and Kashmir found menstruation is still treated as unclean, and that isolating women and limiting them at home harms their emotional and physical wellbeing.

instead: Treat periods as a normal part of health.
Let women decide for themselves whether to take part in rituals and cooking.
Talk about periods openly with boys and girls.

practice: Shutting people out because of caste

why.text: 30% of rural and 20% of urban households said they practise untouchability in some form.
why.source: India Human Development Survey, via NCAER

why.text: 64% of Indians said it is very important to stop women in their community marrying into another caste.
Caste discrimination in India crosses religious lines. Dalit Christians and Dalit Muslims face severe social disadvantage and are left out of Scheduled Caste benefits.

instead: Invite everyone and sit together at every meal and event.
Support couples who marry across caste and religion.
Speak up and report caste discrimination; it is a crime.
